				<div id="bodyContent" class="vector-body" aria-labelledby="firstHeading" data-mw-ve-target-container>
					<div class="vector-body-before-content">
							<div class="mw-indicators">
		</div>

						<div id="siteSub" class="noprint">From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia</div>
					</div>
					<div id="contentSub"><div id="mw-content-subtitle"></div></div>
					
					
					<div id="mw-content-text" class="mw-body-content"><div class="mw-subjectpageheader">
</div><div class="mw-content-ltr mw-parser-output" lang="en" dir="ltr"><div class="shortdescription nomobile noexcerpt noprint searchaux" style="display:none">Canadian adventurer, diarist and author</div>
<p><b>Don Starkell</b> (December 7, 1932 &#8211; January 28, 2012) was a Canadian adventurer, diarist and author, perhaps best known for his achievements in <a href="/wiki/Canoeing" title="Canoeing">canoeing</a>,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> in particular, paddling from <a href="/wiki/Winnipeg" title="Winnipeg">Winnipeg</a> to the mouth of the <a href="/wiki/Amazon_River" title="Amazon River">Amazon River</a> and by kayak through the <a href="/wiki/Northwest_Passage" title="Northwest Passage">Northwest Passage</a>.
</p><p>Born in <a href="/wiki/Winnipeg" title="Winnipeg">Winnipeg</a>, <a href="/wiki/Manitoba" title="Manitoba">Manitoba</a>, he had a difficult childhood including an abusive father, four and a half years in an orphanage, and later with a foster family in <a href="/wiki/North_Kildonan" title="North Kildonan">North Kildonan</a>. He took up canoeing in his teens and at age 17 was named Most Outstanding Novice at the Kildonan Canoe Club.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> He competed professionally as a canoeist, winning 10 out of 12 races that he entered. In 1967, he was a member of the Manitoba team that competed in the <a href="/wiki/Expo_1967" class="mw-redirect" title="Expo 1967">Expo 67</a> <a href="/wiki/Centennial_Voyageur_Canoe_Pageant" title="Centennial Voyageur Canoe Pageant">Centennial Voyageur Canoe Pageant</a> race from <a href="/wiki/Rocky_Mountain_House" title="Rocky Mountain House">Rocky Mountain House</a>, <a href="/wiki/Alberta" title="Alberta">Alberta</a> to <a href="/wiki/Montreal,_Quebec" class="mw-redirect" title="Montreal, Quebec">Montreal, Quebec</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The team won the race after a gruelling effort lasting 104 days.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Starkell suffered serious burns to his legs, as well as smoke inhalation when a fire broke out in his house in Winnipeg in March, 2010.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Paddle_to_the_Amazon"><i>Paddle to the Amazo</i>n</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Don_Starkell&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: Paddle to the Amazon"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>On June 1, 1980, he and his two sons, Dana and Jeff Starkell, set out on an epic canoe journey from Winnipeg to <a href="/wiki/Belem,_Brazil" class="mw-redirect" title="Belem, Brazil">Belem, Brazil</a>. The trip followed the <a href="/wiki/Red_River_of_the_North" title="Red River of the North">Red River</a> to its headwaters south of <a href="/wiki/Fargo,_North_Dakota" title="Fargo, North Dakota">Fargo, North Dakota</a>. From there the canoeists <a href="/wiki/Portage" title="Portage">portaged</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Minnesota_River" title="Minnesota River">Minnesota River</a> and then continued down the <a href="/wiki/Mississippi_River" title="Mississippi River">Mississippi River</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Intracoastal_Waterway" title="Intracoastal Waterway">Intracoastal Waterway</a> at <a href="/wiki/Larose,_Louisiana" title="Larose, Louisiana">Larose, Louisiana</a>. They followed the Waterway south to <a href="/wiki/Port_Isabel,_Texas" title="Port Isabel, Texas">Port Isabel, Texas</a>, where they entered the actual Gulf of Mexico, and then skirted the coast of Mexico to <a href="/wiki/Veracruz" title="Veracruz">Veracruz</a> where they spent three and a half months (November 1980 to mid February 1981) to recover from the journey to date, a journey that had been&#8212;and would continue to be&#8212;fraught with difficulty. By this time, Jeff Starkell had decided to abandon the adventure and Donald and Dana continued on alone.
</p><p>They paddled along the rest of Mexico and Central America to South America. Off the <a href="/wiki/Guajira_Peninsula" title="Guajira Peninsula">Guajira Peninsula</a> in <a href="/wiki/Colombia" title="Colombia">Colombia</a> they were beset by <a href="/wiki/Pirate#Modern_piracy" class="mw-redirect" title="Pirate">modern pirates</a> but escaped. They almost died on the <a href="/wiki/Gulf_of_Coro" class="mw-redirect" title="Gulf of Coro">Gulf of Coro</a>, Venezuela after being trapped on a sandbar by strong headwinds as their food supplies ran out. Eventually, on October 14, 1981 they made land at <a href="/wiki/Port_of_Spain,_Trinidad" class="mw-redirect" title="Port of Spain, Trinidad">Port of Spain, Trinidad</a>, where they recuperated for six weeks.
</p><p>On New Years Day, 1982, they set off from Port of Spain and three days later crossed the <a href="/wiki/Columbus_Channel" title="Columbus Channel">Columbus Channel</a> to Venezuela. There, at <a href="/wiki/Pedernales,_Delta_Amacuro" title="Pedernales, Delta Amacuro">Pedernales</a>, they entered the delta of the <a href="/wiki/Orinoco_River" class="mw-redirect" title="Orinoco River">Orinoco River</a>. Over the next two months they paddled virtually the entire length of the Orinoco to Tama Tama where they entered the <a href="/wiki/Casiquiare_canal" title="Casiquiare canal">Casiquiare canal</a>, the only natural canal in the world. Via this route they reached the <a href="/wiki/Rio_Negro_(Amazon)" title="Rio Negro (Amazon)">Rio Negro</a> and then the <a href="/wiki/Amazon_River" title="Amazon River">Amazon River</a> at <a href="/wiki/Manaus,_Brazil" class="mw-redirect" title="Manaus, Brazil">Manaus, Brazil</a>. From Manaus, they paddled downriver to the <a href="/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean" title="Atlantic Ocean">Atlantic</a> coast. The journey ended at Belem on May 2, 1982.
</p><p>In 1986, the names of Don Starkell and his son Dana were entered into the <i><a href="/wiki/Guinness_Book_of_World_Records" class="mw-redirect" title="Guinness Book of World Records">Guinness Book of World Records</a></i> for having completed the longest canoe journey ever, a distance of 19,603 kilometres (12,181&#160;mi).<sup id="cite&#95;ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>He was inducted into the Manitoba Sports Hall of Fame in 2006 in recognition of his all round athletic excellence.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-7"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Paddle_to_the_Arctic"><i>Paddle to the Arctic</i></h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Don_Starkell&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: Paddle to the Arctic"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>In 1990, Starkell sought to trace the <a href="/wiki/Northwest_Passage" title="Northwest Passage">Northwest Passage</a> by <a href="/wiki/Kayak" title="Kayak">kayak</a>. Though comparatively short&#8212;at 3,000 miles&#8212;the trip was more difficult due to the cold weather. It lasted three years and had to be terminated just thirty miles short of its planned completion point at <a href="/wiki/Tuktoyaktuk" title="Tuktoyaktuk">Tuktoyaktuk</a>, due to the onset of winter and frostbite. Starkell lost the tops of his fingers and some of his toes. "When I did the Arctic trip, I gave absolutely everything I had and that was success," he said.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Publications">Publications</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Don_Starkell&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Publications"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<ul><li>Don Starkell, edited by Charles Wilkins, <i>Paddle to the Amazon</i>, Toronto: McLelland and Stewart, 1987</li>
<li>Don Starkell, <i>Paddle to the Arctic</i>, Toronto: McLelland and Stewart, 1995</li>
<li>Victoria Jason, <i>Kabloona in the Yellow Kayak: One Women's Journey Through the Northwest Passage</i>,  Turnstone Press Limited, 1996. (Account by one of the participants in the Arctic journey)</li></ul>
